content: In mathematics, the total variation of a real-valued function ( f ), defined on an interval that is a subset of ( mathbb{R} ), is the supremum of the sum of absolute differences of ( f ) over all possible partitions of the interval. A function ( f ) is said to have bounded variation if its total variation is finite. The set ( C_c^1(Omega, mathbb{R}^n) ) represents continuously differentiable vector functions with compact support within ( Omega ), and ( Vert cdot Vert_{L^infty(Omega)} ) denotes the essential supremum norm. In probability theory, the total variation distance between two probability measures ( P ) and ( Q ) on a sigma-algebra ( F ) is the maximum possible difference between the probabilities assigned by ( P ) and ( Q ) to the same event. For a finite alphabet, this distance can be expressed as the sum of the absolute differences of the probabilities assigned to each element, divided by two. In some cases, the statistical distance is defined without dividing by two. In measure theory, given a signed measure ( mu ) on a measurable space ( (X, Sigma) ), its variation is the non-negative measure obtained from the Hahn-Jordan decomposition of ( mu ) into the difference of two non-negative measures. The total variation of ( mu ) is defined as the supremum of the sum of ( mu ) over all finite partitions of ( X ) into disjoint measurable subsets. For vector measures, the variation is similarly defined. The total variation norm is a norm on the space of measures of bounded variation, making it a Banach space known as the ( ca )-space. This space is contained within the larger Banach space ( ba )-space, which consists of finitely additive measures (as opposed to countably additive measures) with the same norm. Total variation is a non-negative real-valued functional defined on the space of real-valued functions (for single-variable cases) or on the space of integrable functions (for multi-variable cases). It has applications in various fields of mathematics and engineering, such as optimal control, numerical analysis, and the calculus of variations, where minimizing the total variation is often a key objective. For example, in numerical analysis of differential equations, total variation is used to study methods for approximating solutions to differential equations, particularly in the context of total variation diminishing techniques. In image processing, total variation is applied in image denoising, which involves reducing noise in images reconstructed from data obtained through electronic means, such as data transmission or sensing.
